variants.title: Count encoding and fixed overhead
variants.context: Tokenization consumes CPU for every encoded token plus fixed work per call. In this planning model, encode cores = uncached requests/s × tokens/request ÷ tokens/core/s. Fixed-cost cores = uncached requests/s × fixed milliseconds ÷ 1,000 ÷ batch size. Add both, then divide by usable cores per worker and round up. Ignore cache lookup and network cost.
variants.prompt: Illustrative chat traffic is 9,000 requests/s, 220 tokens/request, with no cache hits. Encoding runs at 720,000 tokens/core/s. Fixed work is 0.32 ms per request, shared across batches of 16. Each worker has 2 cores with a 70% utilization target. What minimum whole worker count meets this estimate?

mistakes.feedback: Two workers provide 2.8 usable cores at the 70% target. The workload needs 2.75 encoding cores plus 0.18 fixed-cost cores: 2.93 in total.
One worker offers only 1.4 usable cores. Batching shares fixed overhead, not all token-encoding work.
Four workers fit but are not the minimum. Add 2.75 and 0.18 cores, then divide by 1.4 and round up once.

variants.explanation: Encoding: 9,000 × 220 ÷ 720,000 = 2.75 cores. Fixed work: 9,000 × 0.00032 ÷ 16 = 0.18 cores. Each worker supplies 2 × 0.70 = 1.4 usable cores, so ceil(2.93 ÷ 1.4) = 3 workers. These teaching constants are not a hardware benchmark; queue and tail behavior still need measurement.
variants.hint: Each worker contributes 1.4 cores at the target. Include the 0.18 cores of fixed work before rounding the worker count.

variants.title: Plan for uncached document work
variants.context: An exact result-cache hit avoids encoding. Assume hits are evenly distributed across input lengths and do not consume encode or fixed-call CPU in this simplified model. Divide uncached token work by tokens/core/s, add uncached requests/s × fixed seconds ÷ batch size, then divide by usable worker cores and round up.
variants.prompt: Document traffic is 1,830 requests/s with a 50% exact cache-hit rate and 1,800 tokens per uncached request. Encoding runs at 610,000 tokens/core/s; fixed work is 0.38 ms shared across batches of 4. Workers have 2 cores at a 70% utilization target. Ignoring cache/network cost, what minimum worker count fits?

mistakes.feedback: One worker has only 1.4 usable cores. Batching does not divide the 2.7 cores of token-encoding work.
That is the estimate when all 1,830 requests miss the cache. Only 915 requests/s need encoding under the stated 50% hit assumption.
Three workers would fit, but two provide 2.8 usable cores, just above the estimated 2.786925-core demand.

variants.explanation: Uncached rate: 1,830 × 0.5 = 915 requests/s. Encoding: 915 × 1,800 ÷ 610,000 = 2.7 cores. Fixed work: 915 × 0.00038 ÷ 4 = 0.086925 cores. ceil(2.786925 ÷ 1.4) = 2 workers. The small margin makes this a planning floor; real cache variance and overhead must be measured before deployment.
variants.hint: Apply the cache-hit rate first. The remaining 915 requests/s contribute both token work and batched fixed overhead.

variants.title: Preserve headroom for a heavier traffic slice
variants.context: Two workloads with the same request count may have different encoded lengths and CPU rates. Use the measured slice's coefficients. Add token-encoding cores and batched fixed-cost cores, then divide by worker cores × target utilization and round up. Ignore cache lookup and network cost here.
variants.prompt: An illustrative multilingual/code slice receives 4,700 requests/s with 760 tokens/request and no cache hits. Encoding rate is 470,000 tokens/core/s. Fixed work is 0.46 ms per request, shared across batches of 8. Each 2-core worker targets 70% utilization. How many workers are required by this model?

mistakes.feedback: Four workers cover the demand only if you ignore the 70% target and plan near full physical CPU use.
Five workers provide 7 usable cores, below 7.87025. Round the worker requirement up, not down.
Dividing token work by batch size incorrectly treats encoding as fixed overhead. Only the 0.46 ms per-call overhead is shared in this model.

variants.explanation: Encoding takes 4,700 × 760 ÷ 470,000 = 7.6 cores. Fixed overhead adds 4,700 × 0.00046 ÷ 8 = 0.27025 cores. ceil(7.87025 ÷ (2 × 0.70)) = 6 workers. Token work by traffic slice gives a more useful starting point than raw request rate.
variants.hint: Token work needs 7.6 cores before overhead. Each worker contributes only 1.4 usable cores at the target.

variants.title: Bound and identify the encode operation
variants.context: A tokenizer's integer IDs are meaningful only for its matching model bundle. Admission protects CPU capacity; the bundle fingerprint identifies the normalizer, vocabulary, special tokens, and template that produced the result.
variants.prompt: Arrange this uncached synchronous request path. A bundle is already warmed; only compatible admitted work may enter its bounded worker queue. The final response must contain checked output bounds and lineage.

items.text: Return checked IDs, masks, requested offsets, and the producing bundle fingerprint.
Resolve the admitted request to its exact approved tokenizer-model bundle and options.
Validate bytes, batch width, requested options, and tenant limits before expensive work.
After encoding, check output-token limits and record any allowed truncation explicitly.
Encode compatible work in the bounded CPU pool with a maximum batch wait.

variants.explanation: Admit → resolve the exact contract → encode bounded work → check output policy → return evidence. Byte bounds protect work before encoding; actual token counts then enforce the output bound. Returning a fingerprint makes the result traceable to the model interface.
variants.hint: Validate the request before work, select the contract before encoding, and check the produced output before returning it.

variants.title: Prove exact compatibility before exposure
variants.context: A release gate verifies known IDs and structural boundaries before checking averages. A complete immutable bundle includes the tokenizer, model, normalization, template, special-token policy, and fingerprints needed to reproduce or roll back behavior.
variants.prompt: Order this staged release. Exact checks must pass before protected-slice evaluation; both must pass before any canary traffic. Keep the previous complete bundle ready throughout.

items.text: After offline gates pass, send bounded traffic to the candidate bundle and observe it.
Run golden-ID, mask, offset, decoding, template, and special-token checks.
Expand traffic only after the canary passes, retaining the rollback contract.
Build and fingerprint the complete immutable tokenizer-model bundle.
After exact checks pass, evaluate expansion, truncation, quality, and latency on protected slices.

variants.explanation: Build → exact checks → protected slices → bounded canary → promotion. Better average token counts cannot compensate for a broken ID or role boundary. Evaluate the whole bundle that will actually receive production traffic.
variants.hint: First make a reproducible candidate, prove its exact contract, measure its protected slices, then expose users gradually.

variants.title: Restore a compatible bundle after drift
variants.context: Rollback must restore the whole model interface. Old token IDs cannot safely be paired with a different embedding table or template. In this runbook, validate the retained bundle and its cache namespace before moving affected traffic.
variants.prompt: A canary produces unexpected special-token IDs. Order recovery under the stated runbook. The previous bundle is retained; do not route requests to it before its exact fixtures and cache identity have been checked.

items.text: Route affected traffic to the verified previous model-tokenizer-template bundle and matching cache namespace.
Verify the retained bundle's exact fixtures and bundle-scoped cache identity.
After recovery, add the failing input as a regression fixture before another release.
Stop canary expansion and record the affected candidate fingerprint.
Confirm restored outputs, fingerprints, and affected-slice behavior after the traffic switch.

variants.explanation: Stop expansion → verify a compatible destination → route the complete bundle → confirm recovery → preserve a regression fixture. Rolling back only weights or only the tokenizer can leave the incompatible pairing intact. Cache reuse must follow the restored contract too.
variants.hint: Contain the change, establish the recovery contract, switch traffic, verify the result, then improve the gate.

variants.title: Do not exchange exact offsets for average savings
variants.context: Normalization can change text identity and source offsets even when it reduces token count. The approved tokenizer contract requires exact fixture outputs; downstream annotation or citation spans rely on the declared offset representation.
variants.prompt: The lesson's normalizer-change candidate reduces the measured token-count statistic by 8.1%, but only 76.2% of golden fixtures and 62.5% of offsets match. The deployed model and offset consumers are unchanged. What should the release gate do?
options: Promote because fewer tokens always make serving better.
Block this drop-in release; treat changed text and offsets as a new contract requiring compatible consumers and approved evidence.
Clear caches and accept the new outputs without changing the gate.
optionFeedback: Average savings do not repair changed input IDs or source spans. The candidate violates the existing exact contract.
The optimization is not behavior-preserving. Compatibility must be established for the full set of model and offset consumers.
Cache invalidation cannot make newly generated mismatching IDs and offsets compatible with unchanged consumers.
variants.explanation: Block the incompatible drop-in change. A legitimate new normalization contract needs approved fixture expectations and compatible downstream behavior, not an exception based on aggregate cost. The reported savings are a teaching scenario, not a general property of normalization.
variants.hint: The original contract includes exact output identity and offsets. Which option protects both?

variants.title: A text hash does not identify an encode result
variants.context: The same bytes can produce different cached results under different bundle revisions, maximum lengths, truncation, padding, special-token settings, or offset contracts. Tenant policy can also prohibit reuse even when the numeric IDs happen to match.
variants.prompt: A cache keyed only by SHA-256(input bytes) returns tenant A's 128-token truncated result to tenant B, which requested an untruncated result up to 512 tokens. Cross-tenant result reuse is prohibited. What fixes the design?
options: Keep the text-only key but increase its expiration time.
Use a stronger hash of the same input bytes without changing any other key fields.
Key by input hash, bundle fingerprint, complete encode/length/offset options, and tenant scope; apply the same scope to access.
optionFeedback: Longer retention extends the lifetime of the incompatible and unauthorized reuse.
The failure is omitted contract and scope fields, not a collision between different input bytes.
This separates both output-changing options and the tenant boundary, preventing this result from satisfying the other request.
variants.explanation: Cache identity must describe the exact output contract and allowed reuse scope. Hashing alone neither captures options nor authorizes sharing. Avoid raw text in keys or logs; cached IDs still require appropriate tenant handling.
variants.hint: Two independent failures occurred: different requested outputs and prohibited cross-tenant reuse.

variants.title: Fail explicitly when no compatible tokenizer is ready
variants.context: Token IDs select learned model embedding rows. Similar vocabulary size or familiar token spellings do not establish that another tokenizer maps input to the IDs and control markers expected by a checkpoint.
variants.prompt: The exact tokenizer artifacts for a pinned model revision fail startup validation. A newer tokenizer has the same vocabulary size but different ID mappings. No verified compatible fallback is loaded. What should the worker do?
options: Remain unready for that bundle and return an explicit unavailable result until a verified compatible bundle is ready.
Serve with the newer tokenizer because the embedding table has the same number of rows.
Remove special tokens and serve with the newer tokenizer until traffic falls.
optionFeedback: This prevents silent model-interface corruption when the required contract is unavailable.
Equal row count does not mean equal row meaning. Remapped IDs can select unrelated embeddings.
Removing control markers creates another contract violation and does not restore the old ID mapping.
variants.explanation: Readiness must prove the requested bundle is compatible, not merely that a tokenizer loads. Recover the approved immutable bundle or a fully verified equivalent. A transport success with incompatible IDs is a correctness failure.
variants.hint: Ask whether the candidate preserves the meaning of every emitted ID and control marker, not whether its vocabulary has the same size.
